# Final Project: ATAC-Seq Nextflow Pipeline Analysis

## [Source of Data:]{.underline}

Publication: De Sá Fernandes C, Novoszel P, Gastaldi T, Krauß D, Lang M, Rica R, Kutschat AP, Holcmann M, Ellmeier W, Seruggia D, Strobl H, Sibilia M. The histone deacetylase HDAC1 controls dendritic cell development and anti-tumor immunity. Cell Rep. 2024 Jun 25;43(6):114308. doi: 10.1016/j.celrep.2024.114308. Epub 2024 Jun 2. PMID: 38829740.

## [Introduction]{.underline}

Dendritic cells (DCs) are specialized immune cells that bridge innate and adaptive immunity by detecting pathogen and tumor antigens, and activating naive T cells in lymph nodes to initiate immune responses. There are two types of DC cells that play a large role in immune responses: conventional DC1 (cDC1) and conventional DC2 (cDC2). The development of cDCs is orchestrated by transcription factors (TFs) such as IRF4, IRF8, and SPIB. However, the epigenetic mechanisms regulating chromatin accessibility and gene expression during DC development are not completely understood. In this study, the researchers focused on the role of histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1), which is an enzyme that modulates chromatin structure and TF accessibility, and has been shown to play a crucial role in the development of immune cells.

The study used ATAC-seq on cDC1 and cDC2 cells from mice, with wild type (WT) and HDAC1 knock-out (KO) samples. ATAC-seq data was used to map chromatin accessibility using Tn5 transposase, identifying regulatory elements such as enhancers and promoters. Linking the changes in chromatin landscape, gene expression, and identifying differentially accessible regions gave the researchers a better understanding of the transcriptional and epigenetic factors governing DC specification in development and function.

## [Methods]{.underline}

ATAC-seq data from GEO accession GSE266584 were analyzed using a Nextflow pipeline. The dataset included eight single-end samples representing two cell types (cDC1 and cDC2), each with wild-type and knockout conditions across two technical replicates. Reference files included adapter sequences, blacklist regions, reference genome, and GTF annotation, which were all specified in the nextflow.config file (exact files in README).

Raw ATAC-seq data was downloaded from NCBI's Sequence Read Archive using SRA Tools v3.2.1 `fasterq-dump` (default parameters). Quality assessment on these reads using FastQC v0.12.1 (default parameters) identified Nextera transposase adapters, which were trimmed using Trimmomatic v0.39 with `ILLUMINACLIP:2:20:7`, `LEADING:3`, `TRAILING:3`, `SLIDINGWINDOW:4:15`, and `MINLEN:20`. These lenient settings avoided over-trimming biologically relevant reads. Post-trimming FastQC confirmed proper adapter removal.

Trimmed reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome (GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa) using Bowtie2 v2.5.4 in `--very-sensitive` mode. Alignment statistics were calculated using Samtools v1.21 `flagstat`, and MultiQC v1.25 aggregated quality control metrics from FastQC, Trimmomatic, and Samtools Flagstat into a single HTML report.

BAM files were sorted using Samtools Sort, then filtered using Samtools View with `-q 30` for high-quality alignments, `-F 4` to remove unmapped reads, and `grep -v chrM` to exclude mitochondrial contamination. Filtered BAM files were indexed using Samtools Index. Homer v4.11 `makeTagDirectory` converted alignments into tag directories for peak calling.

Peak calling was performed using Homer `findPeaks` with `-style histone` for open chromatin regions, and peaks were converted to BED format using Homer `pos2bed`. Consensus peaks were generated using BedTools v2.32.1 `merge`, and read counts were quantified using BedTools `intersect`. BAM files were converted to bigWig format using DeepTools v3.5.5 `bamCoverage`. Signal matrices centered on transcription start sites (TSS) were created using DeepTools `computeMatrix` with `--referencePoint TSS`, `--beforeRegionStartLength 2000`, `--afterRegionStartLength 2000`, `--binSize 10`, and `--missingDataAsZero`.

FRiP scores were calculated by counting unique peak-overlapping reads (BedTools `intersect -u`) divided by total mapped reads. TSS enrichment was calculated using Homer `annotatePeaks` with `-size 4000` and `-hist 10`, computing enrichment as the ratio of average coverage in the +/-100 bp TSS region to background coverage, with scores \>= 7 indicating excellent

Differential accessibility analysis between WT and KO conditions was performed separately for each cell type using DiffBind v3.x with DESeq2. DiffBind analysis included filtered BAM files, individual peak BED files, conditions, and replicates (all cDC1 and cDC2 cell types were considered replicates in DiffBind, although not biological replicates). Consensus peak sets were generated requiring peaks in at least 2 samples (`minOverlap = 2`), with TMM normalization (`score = DBA_SCORE_TMM_MINUS_FULL`). Statistical analysis used DESeq2 (`method = DBA_DESEQ2`, `bBlacklist = FALSE`, `bGreylist = FALSE`) comparing WT versus KO (`categories = DBA_CONDITION`, `minMembers = 2`). Results were filtered at p-value \< 0.01 and categorized into "gain" peaks (positive fold change) and "loss" peaks (negative fold change).

Significant peaks were annotated with genomic features using Homer v4.11 `annotatePeaks.pl`, classifying peaks by genomic context and identifying nearest transcriptional start sites. Enriched motifs were identified using Homer `findMotifsGenome.pl` with `-size 200`, `-mask`, and `-len 8,10,12` to discover transcription factor binding sites. Differential accessibility patterns were visualized using deepTools `computeMatrix reference-point` for heatmap creation (`--referencePoint TSS`, `--beforeRegionStartLength 2000`, `--afterRegionStartLength 2000`, `--binSize 10`). Gain and loss matrices were labeled using `computeMatrixOperations relabel` (`--groupLabels "Gained"` and `--groupLabels "Lost"`), combined using `computeMatrixOperations rbind`, and visualized as heatmaps using `plotHeatmap` with `--sortUsing mean` and `--sortRegions descend`.

## [Quality Control Evaluation]{.underline}

### FASTQC, Trimmomatic, and Flagstat

The ATAC-seq data showed high quality based on FastQC results before and after adapter trimming. Raw data ranged from 18.5M to 24.2M sequences per sample. After Trimmomatic adapter trimming, processed samples maintained 17.3M to 22.8M mapped reads with consistently high mapping rates to the genome ranging from 93.5% to 94.2%. All samples received warnings or failures for the 'Per Base Sequence Content' test due to nucleotide bias at read starts, which is expected in ATAC-seq data from Tn5 transposase insertion preference.

Several samples also failed the 'Sequence Duplication Levels' test, which is typical for ATAC-seq experiments that specifically enrich open chromatin regions at regulatory elements. These duplication patterns reflect that the Tn5 transposase enriched accessible chromatin sites rather than being a concerning technical issue, especially since this is also confirmed by the consistently high mapping rates across all samples.

### ATAC-seq QC Metrics: TSS Enrichment Score and FRiP Score

Fraction of Reads in Peaks (FRiP Scores) measures the proportion of aligned reads that fall within called peaks. A FRiP score over 0.20 means that there was successful open chromatin enrichment. The cDC1 samples showed FRiP scores of 0.29 (WT_1), 0.27 (WT_2), 0.29 (KO_1), and 0.35 (KO_2), while cDC2 samples showed scores of 0.37 (WT_1), 0.27 (WT_2), 0.33 (KO_1), and 0.34 (KO_2). This means that there are more ATAC-seq signals concentrated in regulatory regions versus being scattered randomly across the genome, which indicates the Tn5 transposase successfully targeted open chromatin regions rather than inserting non-specifically into closed chromatin.

TSS (Transcription Start Site) enrichment scores measure the ratio of ATAC-seq signal at transcription start sites compared to background regions across the genome. A TSS enrichment score of \>= 7 indicates "EXCELLENT" quality data with strong signal-to-noise ratio. The cDC1 samples showed TSS enrichment scores of 8.56 (WT_1), 7.99 (WT_2), 8.12 (KO_1), and 9.12 (KO_2), while cDC2 samples showed scores of 7.96 (WT_1), 7.25 (WT_2), 8.00 (KO_1), and 8.50 (KO_2). This means that ATAC-seq signal is strongly concentrated at transcription start sites where chromatin is typically open, which indicates the Tn5 transposase preferentially targeted accessible chromatin at active regulatory regions rather than inserting randomly across the genome, confirming high-quality library preparation with minimal background noise. These excellent TSS enrichment scores across all samples further validate the findings from the FRiP scores, demonstrating consistent experimental quality suitable for reliable downstream differential analysis.

## [Results]{.underline}

### DARs (Differentially Accessible Regions) in the ATAC-seq Data

DiffBind analysis identified 505 significantly differentially accessible regions in cDC1 samples and 265 in cDC2 samples (p \< 0.01), indicating substantial chromatin remodeling in response to the knockout condition, with a more pronounced effect observed in the cDC1 cell type.

### Enrichment of DARs

[cDC1 Enrichment]{.underline}

![](results/enrichr_cdc1.jpg)

[cDC2 Enrichment]{.underline}

![](results/enrichr_cdc2.jpg)

The cDC1 enrichment pathways show a strong enrichment for axon guidance and nervous system development pathways. Even though these pathways are typically associated with neurons, molecules like ephrins and semaphorins are also used by immune cells for migration, positioning, and cell-cell interactions. This suggests that HDAC1 normally keeps these developmental migration programs repressed in mature cDC1 cells, and when HDAC1 is lost, these genes get reactivated, which could disrupt cDC1 migration and their ability to interact with T cells.

The cDC2 enrichment pathways show a strong enrichment for MET receptor signaling pathways. MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in cell migration and survival, and in immune cells, it influences differentiation and tissue localization. This suggests that HDAC1 normally keeps MET signaling pathways repressed in mature cDC2 cells, and when HDAC1 is lost, these genes get reactivated, which could affect cDC2 differentiation, migration, and their ability to respond properly to signals in their environment.

### Motifs from DARs

![cDC1 Homer Motif](results/homer_cdc1.jpg) ![cDC2 Homer Motif](results/homer_cdc2.jpg)

The top Homer motifs for both cDC1 and cDC2 include PU.1 and SPIB, both of which are regulators of DC cell development and control lineage specification and cDC1/cDC2 identity. This suggests that HDAC1 normally keeps these genes' regions controlled, and when HDAC1 is lost, these genomic regions become more accessible, which could allow more PU.1 and SPIB binding and cause problems with gene expression in cDC1/cDC2 cells. This also matches up with what the paper showed—they saw increased ATAC-seq signal at the Spib locus itself in the knockout samples for both cell types, meaning that losing HDAC1 causes both the Spib gene and Spib target sites across the genome to become more accessible.

## [Figure Recreation]{.underline}

### Figure 6A + 6B

[cDC1 Heatmap]{.underline} ![cDC1 heatmap](results/cDC1_differential_heatmap.png) [cDC2 Heatmap]{.underline} ![cDC2 heatmap](results/cDC2_differential_heatmap.png)

My recreation of Figure 6A and 6B accurately displays the same findings as the paper did. Both the cDC1 and cDC2 samples show higher signal near transcription start sites in HDAC1 knockout samples (KO) compared to wild-type (WT), particularly in the "gained" regions. This aligns with what we know about HDAC1 acting as a transcription repressor by compacting chromatin—knocking it out would loosen the chromatin and make it easier for the Tn5 transposase to insert itself into these open regions. This is also why the "loss" region signals are stronger for the WT samples, since chromatin is being compacted by HDAC1, and therefore there is less area for the Tn5 transposase to read the chromatin.

### Figure 6C + 6E

[cDC1 ATAC vs RNA log2fold]{.underline} ![cDC1 ATAC vs RNA log2fold](results/cDC1_ATAC_RNA_integration.png) [cDC2 ATAC vs RNA log2fold]{.underline} ![cDC2 ATAC vs RNA log2fold](results/cDC2_ATAC_RNA_integration.png)

My recreation of Figures 6C and 6E does not align with the paper's figures. The main reason for the discrepancy is that I used normalized RNA-seq count data and manually calculated the log2 fold changes by comparing mean expression between WT and KO, whereas the paper likely used DESeq2 for differential expression analysis. Another factor is how I linked the ATAC-seq peaks to genes. I used Homer AnnotatePeaks to associate differential peaks from DiffBind with nearby genes based on the nearest TSS, which might have made different gene-peak assignments or excluded some genes compared to MACS2 (the method the paper used to call peaks). This could explain why I see fewer genes in the upper-right quadrant (gained accessibility + increased expression). Still, my figures show the same general biological trend: regions with higher chromatin accessibility generally show higher gene expression.

### Figure 6D + 6F

[Maged1 IGV]{.underline} ![Maged1 IGV](results/Maged1_browser_track.png) [SpiB IGV]{.underline} ![SpiB IGV](results/SpiB_browser_track.png)

My recreation of Figure 6D (Maged1) slightly aligned with the paper's figure; however, the difference in peaks between the KO and the WT were not as significant compared to the paper's. A possible reason for this is that the paper could have used replicates and merged them together to create the figure, which makes the signal stronger. Also, it could be possible that using the parameter --style histone for peak calling made my results more conservative, not capturing every possible peak in this area of the genome.

In comparison, Figure 6F does match up with the paper's since the KO samples show stronger peaks throughout the SpiB gene versus the WT samples, which makes sense because the KO of HDAC1 allows for more open chromatin, so more Tn5 transposase can attach to open regions and emit higher signals.
